newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Inventories drop pulled Q4 U.S. GDP lower.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Inventories drop pulled Q4 U.S. GDP lower.

text.p: Lower-than-expected December inventories suggest fourth quarter U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) will be revised sharply lower on Friday and may point to inventories-led growth in the first quarter, analysts said.

Wall Street economists in a recent Reuters poll predicted that GDP grew at a 4.1-percent annualized rate in the fourth quarter, down from the advance report of 4.7 percent but still much higher than the third quarter's 2.1-percent growth rate.
The Commerce Department is set to release revised fourth quarter GDP at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, February 28.

"The lion's share of the revision will be due to substantially lower inventories, which sets the stage for more inventory accumulation in the first quarter," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securties Corp.
Since the last GDP estimate, November business inventories were revised lower and December inventories were reported to have shrunk 0.1 percent.
"We're looking for inventory levels to be cut $13 billion" from those reported in the advance GDP release, Liro said.

While the inventories decline probably dented fourth quarter growth, it could provide a bounce in the first quarter as manufacturers power up to replenish supply stocks. "You've got inventory-to-sales ratios at record lows," said Donald Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc. "If they revise inventory accumulation down further, it would really show how tight inventories are and how susceptible they are to an increase."
The consensus on the first-quarter growth rate appears to have risen to about 3.0 percent, up from the 2.6-percent projection recorded in a late-January Reuters survey.

Other factors besides inventories may contribute to the expected fourth-quarter GDP revision. Personal consumption spending undershot Commerce's previous estimate and the international trade deficit did not improve as much as Commerce had anticipated, some economists said.
"You're going to have a downward revision, a very slight one, in real personal consumption spending because of the downward revision in (December) retail sales," Maude said.
In addition, the previously estimated $37 billion decline in the fourth quarter net exports deficit probably overstated the improvement in the trade balance, CIBC's Liro said.

Because analysts' forecasts of a downward GDP update emerged shortly after the initial report, the Treasury market reaction should be muted if the figure comes in near the forecasters' consensus of 4.1 percent.
"If it's all in inventories there won't be a reaction," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
But any "major downward revisions to other parts, such as consumption," might prompt a positive market reaction, Flanagan said.
Friday's report is unlikely to influence Federal Reserve monetary policy, since GDP is a backward-looking series.
"Lindbergh landed with that stuff," said CIBC's Liro. "The Fed's got its mind focused on forward-looking data, this is ancient history to them."
